target_customer: Law firms and corporate lawyers who proofread contracts
problem: Checking for undefined terms and unused definitions in long legal documents by hand is slow and error prone.
business_model: B2B software licence to law firms, web app or on-site deployment

founders.name: Harry Zhou
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch coverage (seen in search results, not opened) says the idea came from his work as a first-year lawyer proofing a 250 page contract. Second team member not named.

technical_complexity.rationale: Parsing Word documents for defined terms is mostly text processing, with some difficulty in handling varied document formats.

defensibility.rationale: Rule based checks that incumbents in document proofreading could add as a feature.

market_need_then: Lawyers routinely spend associate time on definitions checks; the founder experienced it firsthand per TechCrunch coverage. Customers reported include White & Case, with a trial at Fenwick & West, per a search snippet.

brand_strength.rationale: Unusual capitalisation and spelling variants in press (Springwise printed a different founder surname). No evidence of community around the brand.

outcome_analysis: jEugene built a narrow definitions checker for lawyers, got early law firm interest and a Techcrunch write up at demo day, and recorded only a small funding figure. Directories list it as closed or inactive. No post-mortem or news about the end was found, so the cause is not public.
notes: The $120,000 seed figure comes from the Stanford CodeX TechIndex entry only (a single database); Crunchbase shows a seed tag without an amount; it may be the standard YC deal rather than an outside round. Website did not resolve (DNS failure), treated as dead. A free Defined Terms Checker Word add-in exists but is undated, so it is not listed as a competitor. Founder education and prior employers not found in an opened source.
